title: No one wants to go
hook: one by one the great disciples decline, each remembering being out-argued by him

segments.voice: Yesterday, Vimalakirti lay sick in Vaishali, teaching his visitors that the body is like foam. Your line: the sick layman. Did you ask after someone who's unwell? Day one thousand one hundred eighty-seven.

The Buddha asks a simple favor. Go and ask after Vimalakirti; he's ill. He turns first to Shariputra, the disciple known for wisdom. And Shariputra says, as the sutra tells it: I'm not fit to go. Then he explains why, and the explanation is a story about himself coming off badly. The Buddha turns to the next disciple, and the next. Each one says no. Each one has a story. And every story is told by the one who lost the argument. Today: no one wants to go.
screen: `A SIMPLE FAVOR.` → `I'M NOT FIT TO GO.` → `EACH ONE HAS A STORY.`

segments.voice: Here are a few of the stories, paraphrased. Shariputra remembers sitting quietly under a tree in the forest, deep in meditation. Vimalakirti came by and told him: that isn't the way to sit. Sit so that you don't withdraw from the world. Sit while doing the ordinary things of life. Sit without leaving behind the people around you. Shariputra says he had no answer, so he stayed silent. Maudgalyayana remembers teaching a crowd of householders in the street. Vimalakirti stopped him and said the teaching can't be handed out the way he was handing it out. Mahakashyapa remembers going only to poor houses for alms, to give the poor a chance to earn merit. Vimalakirti told him to beg from everyone alike, rich and poor. And then Ananda. The Buddha had been unwell, and Ananda went to a house to fetch some milk. Vimalakirti met him at the door and said, hush, the Buddha's body is the body of the teaching; don't let anyone hear you say he's sick. Ananda was mortified. Then a voice from the sky said: Ananda, the layman is right. But go and take the milk, and don't be ashamed. Look at what the sutra is doing. These are the great disciples, the names at the center of the older discourses, and here each one remembers being out-argued by a householder. And they say so, in front of everyone. Then even the bodhisattvas decline, Maitreya among them. The sutra is clearing the room for someone. Each refusal makes the visit sound harder.
screen: `SHARIPUTRA UNDER A TREE.` · `KASHYAPA AT THE POOR HOUSES.` · `ANANDA AND THE MILK.` · `THE GREAT DISCIPLES ADMIT IT.` · then, large: `THEY ALL DECLINED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: admit one time you were out-argued. Settle, and breathe. Let a memory come, any memory, of someone getting the better of you in a conversation. A sibling. A teacher. A child who asked a question you couldn't answer. Notice how it feels in the body, maybe a little heat in the face. Now do what the disciples did. Say to yourself, plainly: they were right, and I had no answer. Then let the breath carry the rest. Nobody else needs to hear it. The bell holds the time.
No one wants to go. One by one the Buddha's great disciples decline to visit Vimalakirti, each remembering the day he left them speechless. Today's word.
screen: `NO ONE WANTS TO GO — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: they all declined. Today, when someone corrects you and they're right, say so out loud, the way the disciples did. Day one thousand one hundred eighty-seven.

howItsDone: Some teachers in Mahayana traditions use these refusal stories to teach that practice is not limited to the forest or the meditation hall, and that a layperson's insight can match a monk's.

fork.setup: you're Shariputra. the Buddha asks you to visit Vimalakirti, the layman who once corrected you while you sat in the forest. what do you do?
options: go gladly, ready for a rematch.
decline, and tell everyone the story of being out-argued.
send a gift instead and say you're busy.
fork.reveal: he says he's not fit to go, and tells the story against himself, in front of everyone. the others do the same.

original.note: Sanskrit: Shariputra, the disciple known for wisdom, the first to decline.

trapdoor: what you thought: a list of excuses.
what it means: each great disciple declines by confessing the day Vimalakirti left him without an answer.
what a scholar hears: the sutra lets the famous disciples of the older discourses tell stories against themselves, to clear the stage for the bodhisattva Manjushri.

notes: Paraphrased from the Vimalakirti-nirdesha ch. 3 (the disciples) and ch. 4 (the bodhisattvas); no translation quoted.

Episodes used: Shariputra's sitting in the forest; Maudgalyayana teaching householders; Mahakashyapa begging only from the poor; Ananda and the milk with the voice from the sky. Confirm each, especially the Ananda wording ('the layman is right, but take the milk and don't be ashamed').
Mahakashyapa's reason (to give the poor a chance to earn merit) is the usual reading; confirm.
Hook says each story is told by the one who lost the argument; confirm.

The framing that the sutra lets the older disciples come off badly could read as a polemic against Theravada; it's phrased as the sutra's own move, not a judgment. Keeper should confirm the tone is fair.
